name: Joshua
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls of Joshua (4QJosh-a and 4QJosh-b). The Old Greek of Joshua often differs from the Hebrew. It is shorter in many places, it places the altar on Mount Ebal (8:30–35) after 9:2, and it adds material, most notably after 24:31 and 24:33. The major differences are given in the footnotes. Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a places the reading of the Law (8:34–35) right after the Jordan crossing, before 5:2. This was checked against published descriptions of the scroll (Ulrich), and other scroll readings are stated in general terms. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible. Measurements are given in modern US units, and calendar dates with their modern-month equivalents, with the originals and metric figures in the footnotes. Place names whose meaning is known or likely have a note at their first appearance.

verses.text: After the death of Moses the servant of Yahweh, Yahweh said to Joshua{a} the son of Nun,{b} Moses’ assistant,
“Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, cross over this Jordan,{c} you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the Israelites.
Every place on which the sole of your foot treads I have given to you, as I promised Moses.

From the wilderness and this Lebanon{d} as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and as far as the Great Sea{e} toward the setting of the sun, will be your territory.
No one will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you or forsake you.
Be strong and courageous, for you will cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.

Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may prosper{f} wherever you go.

This book of the law must not depart from your mouth, but you are to meditate{g} on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will succeed.
Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be terrified or dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people, saying,

“Pass through the middle of the camp and command the people, saying, ‘Prepare provisions for yourselves, for within three days you are to cross over this Jordan, to go in to take possession of the land that Yahweh your God is giving you to possess.’”
To the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,
“Remember the word that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, saying, ‘Yahweh your God is giving you rest and will give you this land.’

Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock may remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan,{h} but all your mighty men of valor are to cross over armed{i} before your brothers and help them,

until Yahweh gives your brothers rest as he has given you, and they also take possession of the land that Yahweh your God is giving them. Then you may return to the land of your possession and possess it, the land that Moses the servant of Yahweh gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise.”
They answered Joshua, saying, “All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.
Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may Yahweh your God be with you as he was with Moses.
Whoever rebels against your command and does not obey your words in all that you command him will be put to death. Only be strong and courageous.”

notes.text: Hebrew Yehoshua‘, “Yahweh is salvation” (or “Yahweh saves”). His earlier name was Hoshea, “salvation” (Numbers 13:16). The Greek form of the name is Iesous, “Jesus.”
Nun may mean “fish.” The Septuagint spells it Naue.
Hebrew Yarden, probably “the one that goes down,” fitting the river’s steep descent to the Dead Sea.
Lebanon means “white,” perhaps from its snowy peaks or limestone cliffs. The Septuagint reads “Antilibanus.”
That is, the Mediterranean Sea.
Or “act wisely”; so in verse 8.
Hebrew hagah, to murmur or read in an undertone (compare Psalm 1:2).
That is, east of the Jordan.
Or “in battle formation”; the Hebrew ḥamushim is related to the word for “five,” perhaps describing an army in five divisions.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men as spies from Shittim,{a} saying, “Go, look over the land, especially Jericho.”{b} So they went and came into the house of a prostitute{c} whose name was Rahab,{d} and lodged there.
It was told the king of Jericho, “Look, men from the Israelites have come here tonight to search out the land.”
So the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land.”
But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. She said, “Yes, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.
When the gate was about to be shut at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them.”
But she had brought them up to the roof and hidden them under the stalks of flax that she had laid out on the roof.
So the men pursued them on the road to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out after them.
Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof
and said to the men, “I know that Yahweh has given you the land, and that the terror of you has fallen on us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.

For we have heard how Yahweh dried up the water of the Red Sea{e} before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.{f}
When we heard it, our hearts melted, and no courage remained in anyone because of you, for Yahweh your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
Now then, please swear to me by Yahweh, since I have dealt kindly with you, that you also will deal kindly with my father’s house, and give me a sure sign,
that you will spare my father and my mother, my brothers and my sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death.”
The men said to her, “Our life for yours, even to death!{g} If you do not tell this business of ours, then when Yahweh gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you.”
Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was in the town wall, and she lived in the wall.
She said to them, “Go into the hill country, so that the pursuers do not meet you. Hide there three days until the pursuers have returned, and afterward you may go on your way.”
The men said to her, “We will be free from this oath of yours that you have made us swear,

unless, when we come into the land, you tie this cord of scarlet thread in the window through which you let us down, and gather into your house your father and your mother, your brothers, and all your father’s household.

If anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood will be on his own head, and we will be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood will be on our head.
But if you tell this business of ours, then we will be free from your oath that you have made us swear.”
She said, “According to your words, so be it.” Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
They went and came into the hill country and stayed there three days, until the pursuers returned. The pursuers searched all along the way but did not find them.
Then the two men returned. They came down from the hill country, crossed over, and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.
They said to Joshua, “Truly Yahweh has given all the land into our hands, and all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.”

notes.text: Shittim means “acacia trees” (Numbers 25:1).
Jericho may mean “moon city,” from yareaḥ, “moon,” or “fragrant place,” from reaḥ, “scent.” The meaning is uncertain.

Hebrew zonah. Josephus and the Aramaic Targum understood her as an innkeeper, but the Hebrew word means “prostitute,” as the Septuagint (pornē) and the New Testament (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25) take it.
Rahab means “broad” or “wide.” She appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Hebrew ḥaram, to give something over completely to Yahweh, usually by destroying it. See the note at 6:17.
Literally “Our life in place of yours, to die.”

verses.text: Joshua rose early in the morning, and they set out from Shittim and came to the Jordan, he and all the Israelites, and they lodged there before they crossed over.
At the end of three days the officers went through the middle of the camp
and commanded the people, saying, “When you see the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you are to set out from your place and follow it.
Yet there is to be a distance between you and it of about 3,000 feet{a} by measure. Do not come near it, so that you may know the way you are to go, for you have not passed this way before.”
Joshua said to the people, “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow Yahweh will do wonders among you.”
Joshua said to the priests, “Take up the ark of the covenant and cross over before the people.” So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.
You are to command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant, ‘When you come to the edge of the waters of the Jordan, you are to stand still in the Jordan.’”
Joshua said to the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of Yahweh your God.”

Joshua said, “By this you will know that the living God is among you, and that he will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.
Look, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is crossing over before you into the Jordan.
Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one man from each tribe.

When the soles of the feet of the priests who carry the ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan will be cut off, the waters coming down from above, and they will stand in one heap.”
So when the people set out from their tents to cross over the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark of the covenant before the people,

and as soon as those carrying the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests carrying the ark were dipped in the edge of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks all the days of harvest),{b}

the waters coming down from above stood still and rose up in one heap very far away, at Adam,{c} the city that is beside Zarethan,{d} and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea,{e} were completely cut off. And the people crossed over opposite Jericho.

The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of Yahweh stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel was crossing over on dry ground, until all the nation had finished crossing over the Jordan.

notes.text: Hebrew “two thousand cubits,” about 900 meters.
That is, the barley and wheat harvest in spring (April–May), when the Jordan was swollen with rain and melting snow from Mount Hermon. Compare 4:19.

Adam means “red” or “earth,” perhaps from the color of its soil. It is probably Tell ed-Damiyeh, about 18 miles (30 kilometers) north of Jericho. Medieval Arabic sources report that landslides there blocked the Jordan in A.D. 1267, and an earthquake did so again in 1927. The Hebrew reads “at Adam,” following the qere (the reading tradition); the written text has “in Adam.”
The location of Zarethan is uncertain.
That is, the Dead Sea.

verses.text: When all the nation had finished crossing over the Jordan, Yahweh said to Joshua,
“Take for yourselves twelve men from the people, one man from each tribe,

and command them, saying, ‘Take up for yourselves twelve stones from here, out of the middle of the Jordan, from the place where the priests’ feet stood firm, and carry them over with you and lay them down at the place where you lodge tonight.’”
Then Joshua called the twelve men whom he had appointed from the Israelites, one man from each tribe.

Joshua said to them, “Cross over before the ark of Yahweh your God into the middle of the Jordan, and each of you lift a stone on his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the Israelites,
so that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’

you are to tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of Yahweh. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones are to be a memorial to the Israelites forever.”

The Israelites did just as Joshua commanded. They took up twelve stones out of the middle of the Jordan, as Yahweh told Joshua, according to the number of the tribes of the Israelites, and carried them over with them to the place where they lodged, and laid them down there.
Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan,{a} in the place where the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood, and they are there to this day.

The priests carrying the ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until everything was finished that Yahweh commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people crossed over in haste.
When all the people had finished crossing over, the ark of Yahweh and the priests crossed over before the people.
The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over armed before the Israelites, as Moses had told them.
About forty thousand armed for war crossed over before Yahweh for battle, to the plains of Jericho.
On that day Yahweh exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they revered him, just as they had revered Moses, all the days of his life.
Yahweh said to Joshua,
“Command the priests carrying the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan.”
So Joshua commanded the priests, saying, “Come up out of the Jordan.”

When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of Yahweh came up from the middle of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests’ feet were lifted up onto dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and ran over all its banks as before.
The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month (in March–April),{b} and they camped at Gilgal{c} on the east border of Jericho.
Those twelve stones that they had taken out of the Jordan Joshua set up at Gilgal.
He said to the Israelites, “When your children ask their fathers in time to come, ‘What are these stones?’
then you are to let your children know, ‘Israel crossed over this Jordan on dry ground.’
For Yahweh your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you until you had crossed over, as Yahweh your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up before us until we had crossed over,
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of Yahweh is mighty, and that you may fear Yahweh your God forever.”

notes.text: Or “Joshua set up the twelve stones that had been in the middle of the Jordan.” The Septuagint reads “other twelve stones,” and the Latin Vulgate also speaks of a second set in the riverbed.

Hebrew “in the first month,” counted from the spring new year of Israel’s religious calendar (Exodus 12:2). It was called Abib and later Nisan. Because the Hebrew months were lunar, it fell in March–April. The tenth day was the day the Passover lamb was chosen (Exodus 12:3).
Gilgal means “circle,” probably a circle of stones. Joshua 5:9 links the name with galal, “to roll away.”

verses.text: When all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan westward, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that Yahweh had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the Israelites until we{a} had crossed over, their hearts melted, and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the Israelites.
At that time{b} Yahweh said to Joshua, “Make for yourself flint knives and circumcise the Israelites again, a second time.”
So Joshua made flint knives for himself and circumcised the Israelites at Gibeath-haaraloth.{c}
This is the reason Joshua circumcised them: all the people who came out of Egypt, the males, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they came out of Egypt.
For all the people who came out had been circumcised, but all the people who were born in the wilderness on the way as they came out of Egypt had not been circumcised.

For the Israelites walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of Yahweh. Yahweh swore to them that he would not let them see the land that Yahweh had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.{d}
So it was their sons, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised, for they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.
When they had finished circumcising all the nation, they stayed in their places in the camp until they were healed.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away{e} the reproach of Egypt from you.” So the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.
While the Israelites were camped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month (in March–April),{f} at evening, in the plains of Jericho.
On the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and roasted grain.{g}
The manna ceased on the next day, when they ate of the produce of the land, and there was no longer manna for the Israelites, but they ate of the yield of the land of Canaan that year.

When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and there was a man standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, “Are you for us or for our adversaries?”
He said, “No, but I have come now as commander of the army of Yahweh.” And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped, and said to him, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
The commander of Yahweh’s army said to Joshua, “Take off your sandal from your foot, for the place where you are standing is holy.” And Joshua did so.

notes.text: So the Hebrew written text (ketiv). The qere (the reading tradition), many Hebrew manuscripts, and the ancient versions read “they.”

The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a (about 150–50 B.C.) is arranged differently here. In it, the end of the account of the reading of the Law (8:34–35) comes right before this verse, linked by a transitional sentence not found in other witnesses. In that order, the covenant reading, and perhaps the building of the altar, took place at Gilgal right after the Jordan crossing. Josephus (Antiquities 5.16–20) also places an altar soon after the crossing. Compare the note at 8:30.
Gibeath-haaraloth means “hill of the foreskins.”
In verses 4–6 the Septuagint has a different text. It says that some of those who came out of Egypt had been uncircumcised, and that Israel wandered forty-two years in the wilderness.
Hebrew galal, which sounds like Gilgal; see the note at 4:19.

Hebrew “on the fourteenth day of the month,” that is, the first month of the spring-start religious calendar (4:19). It was called Abib or Nisan and fell in March–April. The exact correspondence varies from year to year with the lunar calendar.
The Septuagint lacks “on the day after the Passover.”

verses.text: Now Jericho was shut up tight because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “See, I have given into your hand Jericho and its king, the mighty men of valor.
You are to march around the city, all the men of war, going around the city once. You are to do this for six days.
Seven priests are to carry seven trumpets of rams’ horns{a} before the ark. On the seventh day you are to march around the city seven times, and the priests are to blow the trumpets.

When they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people are to shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat,{b} and the people are to go up, each man straight before him.”
So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, “Take up the ark of the covenant, and let seven priests carry seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark of Yahweh.”
He{c} said to the people, “Go forward. March around the city, and let the armed men pass on before the ark of Yahweh.”

Just as Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests carrying the seven trumpets of rams’ horns before Yahweh went forward and blew the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of Yahweh following them.
The armed men went before the priests who blew the trumpets, and the rear guard went after the ark, with the trumpets blowing continually.
But Joshua commanded the people, “You are not to shout or let your voice be heard, nor let a word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout.”
So he had the ark of Yahweh go around the city, circling it once. Then they came into the camp and lodged in the camp.
Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of Yahweh.

The seven priests carrying the seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark of Yahweh walked on, blowing the trumpets continually. The armed men went before them, and the rear guard came after the ark of Yahweh, with the trumpets blowing continually.
On the second day they marched around the city once and returned to the camp. They did this for six days.
On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawning of the day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. Only on that day did they march around the city seven times.
At the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, “Shout, for Yahweh has given you the city.
The city and all that is in it are to be devoted{d} to Yahweh for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in the house will live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.

But as for you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, so that you do not devote them and then take any of the devoted things, and make the camp of Israel something devoted to destruction and bring trouble{e} on it.
But all silver and gold, and vessels of bronze and iron, are holy to Yahweh. They are to go into the treasury of Yahweh.”

So the people shouted, and they blew the trumpets. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, and the people went up into the city, each man straight before him, and they captured the city.
They devoted to destruction all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
Joshua said to the two men who had spied out the land, “Go into the prostitute’s house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her.”

So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab, her father, her mother, her brothers, and all who belonged to her. They brought out all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.
They burned the city with fire and all that was in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and iron, they put into the treasury of the house of Yahweh.

But Rahab the prostitute and her father’s household and all who belonged to her, Joshua spared. She has lived in the midst of Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.

Joshua made them take an oath at that time, saying, “Cursed before Yahweh be the man who rises up and builds this city, Jericho. With the loss of his firstborn he will lay its foundation, and with the loss of his youngest son he will set up its gates.”{f}
So Yahweh was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.

notes.text: Hebrew shofarot hayyovelim, “ram’s-horn trumpets”; the word yovel, “ram,” also gave its name to the Jubilee (Leviticus 25).
Literally “will fall in its place.”
So the qere (the reading tradition), the Septuagint, and other witnesses. The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “They.”
Hebrew ḥerem, something given over completely to Yahweh, which could not be used by people. In war this usually meant its total destruction; so throughout this book.
Hebrew ‘akhar, “trouble”; compare the Valley of Achor in 7:26.

The Septuagint adds, “And so did Hozan of Bethel. He laid its foundation with Abiron his firstborn, and set up its gates with his youngest surviving son.” Compare the fulfillment in 1 Kings 16:34, where the builder is Hiel of Bethel and his sons are Abiram and Segub.

verses.text: But the Israelites acted unfaithfully in regard to the devoted things, for Achan{a} the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi,{b} the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of Yahweh burned against the Israelites.
Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai,{c} which is near Beth-aven,{d} east of Bethel,{e} and said to them, “Go up and spy out the land.” So the men went up and spied out Ai.
They returned to Joshua and said to him, “Do not let all the people go up. Let about two or three thousand men go up and strike Ai. Do not make all the people toil up there, for they are few.”
So about three thousand men from the people went up there, but they fled before the men of Ai.

The men of Ai struck down about thirty-six of them, and chased them from before the gate as far as Shebarim,{f} and struck them down on the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became like water.
Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell on his face to the earth before the ark of Yahweh until the evening, he and the elders of Israel, and they put dust on their heads.

Joshua said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us? If only we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!
O Lord, what can I say, now that Israel has turned their backs before their enemies?
For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it, and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?”
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?

Israel has sinned. They have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them. They have taken some of the devoted things. They have stolen and also deceived, and they have also put them among their own belongings.

Therefore the Israelites cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted to destruction. I will not be with you anymore unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.

Get up, consecrate the people, and say, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, for thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel: “There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you.”

In the morning you are to come near by your tribes. The tribe that Yahweh takes{g} is to come near by clans, the clan that Yahweh takes is to come near by households, and the household that Yahweh takes is to come near man by man.

The one who is taken with the devoted things is to be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of Yahweh and because he has done an outrageous thing{h} in Israel.’”
So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near by tribes, and the tribe of Judah was taken.
He brought near the clans of Judah, and he took the clan of the Zerahites. He brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man,{i} and Zabdi was taken.
He brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.
Then Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and give praise to him.{j} Tell me now what you have done. Do not hide it from me.”
Achan answered Joshua, “Truly I have sinned against Yahweh, the God of Israel, and this is what I did:

When I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar,{k} and about 5 pounds of silver{l} and a bar of gold weighing about 20 ounces,{m} I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the ground inside my tent, with the silver underneath.”
So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent, and there it was, hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.
They took them from the middle of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the Israelites, and they laid them out before Yahweh.

Then Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons, his daughters, his oxen, his donkeys, his sheep, his tent, and all that he had, and they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.
Joshua said, “Why have you brought trouble on us? Yahweh will bring trouble on you today.” And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.
They raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then Yahweh turned from his burning anger. Therefore the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor{n} to this day.

notes.text: The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 2:7 call him Achar, “trouble,” which makes a wordplay with the Valley of Achor (verses 25–26).
The Septuagint has Zambri; 1 Chronicles 2:6 has Zimri.
Ai (Hebrew ha‘ai, always with the article) means “the ruin” or “the heap.”
Beth-aven means “house of wickedness” (or “of nothingness”). Hosea 4:15 later uses the name mockingly for Bethel.
Bethel means “house of God” (Genesis 28:19).
Or “the quarries”; the Hebrew word means “breakings.”
That is, the tribe that is selected, probably by casting the lot.
Or “a disgraceful folly” (Hebrew nevalah).
Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read “by households,” as in verse 14.
Or “and make confession to him.” This was a formula calling someone to tell the truth under oath (compare John 9:24).
That is, Babylonia. The Septuagint reads “an embroidered cloak.”
Hebrew “200 shekels,” about 2.3 kilograms.
Hebrew “50 shekels,” about 575 grams. Literally “a tongue of gold,” that is, a wedge-shaped ingot.
Achor means “trouble.” Compare Hosea 2:15 and Isaiah 65:10, where the valley becomes a place of hope.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Joshua, “Do not fear or be dismayed. Take all the men of war with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land.
You are to do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you may take as plunder for yourselves. Set an ambush against the city behind it.”
So Joshua and all the men of war arose to go up to Ai. Joshua chose thirty thousand mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.
He commanded them, “See, you are to lie in ambush against the city, behind the city. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you be ready.
I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. When they come out against us as at the first, we will flee before them.
They will come out after us until we have drawn them away from the city, for they will say, ‘They are fleeing from us as at the first.’ So we will flee before them.
Then you are to rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for Yahweh your God will give it into your hand.
When you have taken the city, you are to set the city on fire. You are to do according to the word of Yahweh. See, I have commanded you.”
So Joshua sent them out, and they went to the place of ambush and stayed between Bethel and Ai, west of Ai. But Joshua spent that night among the people.
Joshua rose early in the morning and mustered the people, and he went up, with the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.
All the men of war who were with him went up and drew near and came before the city, and they camped north of Ai, with the valley between them and Ai.
He took about five thousand men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, west of the city.
So they stationed the people, all the camp that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. And Joshua went that night into the middle of the valley.{a}

When the king of Ai saw this, the men of the city hurried and rose early and went out to meet Israel in battle, he and all his people, at the appointed place{b} before the Arabah. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.
Joshua and all Israel let themselves be beaten before them and fled by the way of the wilderness.
All the people who were in the city{c} were called together to pursue them, and they pursued Joshua and were drawn away from the city.
Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel{d} who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.
Then Yahweh said to Joshua, “Stretch out the javelin{e} that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand.” And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.
The ambush rose quickly out of its place, and they ran as soon as he had stretched out his hand. They entered the city and captured it, and they quickly set the city on fire.

When the men of Ai looked back, they saw the smoke of the city going up to the heavens, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who had fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.
When Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city and that the smoke of the city was going up, they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.

The others came out from the city against them, so they were in the middle of Israel, some on this side and some on that side. And they struck them down until there was left none that survived or escaped.
But the king of Ai they took alive and brought him to Joshua.

When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open country, in the wilderness where they had pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it with the edge of the sword.
All who fell that day, both men and women, were twelve thousand, all the people of Ai.
For Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.{f}
Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as plunder for themselves, according to the word of Yahweh that he commanded Joshua.
So Joshua burned Ai and made it a heap{g} forever, a desolation to this day.

He hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. At sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the city gate, and raised over it a great heap of stones that remains to this day.
Then Joshua built an altar{h} to Yahweh, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,{i}

as Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded the Israelites, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses, an altar of uncut stones on which no one had wielded an iron tool. They offered burnt offerings on it to Yahweh and sacrificed peace offerings.
There, in the presence of the Israelites, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.

All Israel, sojourner as well as native-born, with their elders, officers, and judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim{j} and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel.
Afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the book of the law.
There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the sojourners who were living among them.

notes.text: Some Hebrew manuscripts read “spent that night” (compare verse 9). The Septuagint lacks most of verses 11b–13; it does not mention the second ambush of five thousand men.
Hebrew mo‘ed; or, with a small change, “at the descent.” The Septuagint lacks this phrase.
The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “in the city”; the qere (the reading tradition) reads “in Ai.”
The Septuagint lacks “or Bethel.”
Or “scimitar” (Hebrew kidon); a curved sword is possible. The Septuagint reads “spear.”
The Septuagint lacks this verse.
Hebrew tel, a mound of ruins, the word that gave its name to the archaeological “tell.” The name Ai means “the ruin” (see the note at 7:2).

The Hebrew text places the altar and the covenant reading on Mount Ebal (verses 30–35) here. The Septuagint places them after 9:2. The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a apparently placed at least the reading of the Law (verses 34–35) right after the Jordan crossing, before 5:2 (see the note there). These different placements suggest that the passage was positioned differently in different early forms of the text. Compare Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:1–26.
Ebal may mean “bare” or “stony.” Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim stand on either side of Shechem.
Gerizim may mean “those cut off.” The Samaritans later regarded it as the chosen place of worship (compare John 4:20).

verses.text: When all the kings who were beyond the Jordan heard of this, those in the hill country, in the lowland,{a} and all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites,
they gathered together with one accord to fight against Joshua and Israel.{b}
But when the inhabitants of Gibeon{c} heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,
they also acted craftily. They went and disguised themselves as envoys,{d} and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins that were worn-out, torn, and mended,
with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet and worn-out clothes on them. And all the bread of their provisions was dry and crumbly.
They went to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, “We have come from a distant country. Now therefore make a covenant with us.”
But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, “Perhaps you live among us. Then how can we make a covenant with you?”
They said to Joshua, “We are your servants.” And Joshua said to them, “Who are you, and where do you come from?”
They said to him, “From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of Yahweh your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt,
and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon king of Heshbon and to Og king of Bashan, who was at Ashtaroth.

So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, ‘Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, “We are your servants. Now therefore make a covenant with us.”’
This bread of ours was warm when we took it from our houses as our provision on the day we set out to come to you, but now, see, it is dry and crumbly.
These wineskins were new when we filled them, and see, they are torn. And these clothes and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey.”
So the men took some of their provisions, but they did not ask counsel from the mouth of Yahweh.
Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them.
At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.
So the Israelites set out and came to their cities on the third day. Their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.{e}
But the Israelites did not strike them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by Yahweh, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation grumbled against the leaders.
But all the leaders said to all the congregation, “We have sworn to them by Yahweh, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them.
This is what we will do to them: we will let them live, so that wrath may not be upon us because of the oath that we swore to them.”
The leaders said to them, “Let them live.” So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.
Joshua summoned them and said to them, “Why did you deceive us, saying, ‘We are very far from you,’ when you live among us?
Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you will never cease to be slaves, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God.”

They answered Joshua, “Because it was clearly told to your servants that Yahweh your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land before you, we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.
Now, see, we are in your hand. Do to us whatever seems good and right in your sight.”
So he did this to them: he delivered them out of the hand of the Israelites, and they did not kill them.
That day Joshua made them cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of Yahweh, to this day, at the place that he would choose.

notes.text: Hebrew shephelah, the low foothills between the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain.

Here the Septuagint has the account of the altar on Mount Ebal and the reading of the Law (Hebrew 8:30–35), as 9:2a–f. In it the passage begins, “Then Joshua built an altar to the Lord, the God of Israel, on Mount Gaibal.” See the note at 8:30.
Gibeon means “hill” or “hilltop place” (from giv‘ah, “hill”). It is probably el-Jib, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

The Hebrew word is uncertain. With a one-letter difference, some Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient versions read “they took provisions” (compare verse 12). The Septuagint reads “they made provision and prepared themselves.”
Kiriath-jearim means “city of forests.” Beeroth means “wells,” and Chephirah may mean “village” or “lioness.”

verses.text: When Adoni-zedek{a} king of Jerusalem{b} heard that Joshua had captured Ai and devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,
he{c} feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty.
So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron,{d} to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon,{e} saying,
“Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon, for it has made peace with Joshua and with the Israelites.”

Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered together and went up, they and all their armies, and camped against Gibeon and fought against it.

The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, saying, “Do not withdraw your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who live in the hill country have gathered against us.”
So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hand. Not a man of them will stand before you.”
So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched all night from Gilgal.

Yahweh threw them into a panic before Israel, and he{f} struck them with a great slaughter at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon,{g} and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they fled before Israel, while they were going down the descent of Beth-horon, Yahweh threw down great stones from the heavens on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword.

Then Joshua spoke to Yahweh on the day when Yahweh gave the Amorites over to the Israelites, and he said in the sight of Israel,{h} “Sun, be still{i} at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon.”{j}

And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?{k} The sun stopped in the middle of the heavens and did not hurry to go down for about a whole day.{l}
There has been no day like it before it or after it, when Yahweh listened to the voice of a man, for Yahweh fought for Israel.
Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.{m}
These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.
It was told to Joshua, “The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah.”
Joshua said, “Roll great stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them.
But do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies and attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for Yahweh your God has given them into your hand.”
When Joshua and the Israelites had finished striking them with a very great slaughter until they were wiped out, and the survivors who remained of them had entered the fortified cities,
all the people returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. No one moved his tongue against any of the Israelites.
Then Joshua said, “Open the mouth of the cave and bring out to me these five kings from the cave.”
They did so and brought out to him these five kings from the cave: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.

When they brought these kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, “Come near, put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So they came near and put their feet on their necks.
Joshua said to them, “Do not fear or be dismayed. Be strong and courageous, for this is what Yahweh will do to all your enemies against whom you fight.”
Afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. They hung on the trees until evening.

At the time of sunset Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set great stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.

Joshua captured Makkedah on that day and struck it and its king with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it. He left no survivor. He did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.

Yahweh gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. He struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it. He left no survivor in it, and he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish, and camped against it and fought against it.
Yahweh gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, according to all that he had done to Libnah.
Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish, and Joshua struck him and his people until he left him no survivor.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon, and they camped against it and fought against it.
They captured it on that day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and he devoted every person in it to destruction on that day, according to all that he had done to Lachish.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron, and they fought against it.

They captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns and every person in it. He left no survivor, according to all that he had done to Eglon, and he devoted it and every person in it to destruction.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir{n} and fought against it.

He captured it with its king and all its towns, and they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted every person in it to destruction. He left no survivor. As he had done to Hebron, and as he had done to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and its king.

So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country, the Negev,{o} the lowland, and the slopes, and all their kings. He left no survivor, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, as Yahweh, the God of Israel, commanded.
Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea{p} as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen as far as Gibeon.
Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because Yahweh, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.
Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.

notes.text: Adoni-zedek means “my lord is righteous” (or “my lord is Zedek,” a divine name). Compare Melchizedek, king of Salem (Genesis 14:18). The Septuagint reads Adonibezek (compare Judges 1:5–7).
The meaning of Jerusalem is uncertain; it is perhaps “foundation of Shalem,” the name of a god, though it was later understood as “city of peace.”
Hebrew “they.”
Hebron may mean “alliance” or “association.” It was earlier called Kiriath-arba (14:15).
The Septuagint reads “Dabin king of Odollam” (that is, Adullam) here and in verses 5 and 23, though it has Eglon in verses 34–37.
That is, Joshua (or Israel).
Beth-horon probably means “house of Horon,” a Canaanite god, or perhaps “house of the hollow.” The road climbed from the coastal lowland through Upper and Lower Beth-horon.
The Hebrew can also mean “and he said, in the sight of Israel.” The Septuagint reads only “and Joshua said.”

Hebrew dom, “be still, be silent,” or “stop.” Some interpreters take the poetry as a request that the sun stop shining (cease its scorching heat, or be darkened by the storm of verse 11) rather than stop moving. The lines are poetry, and the prose that follows takes them literally.

Aijalon means “place of deer” (from ’ayyal, “deer”). The valley lies west of Gibeon, so the sun stood over Gibeon to the east and the moon over Aijalon to the west, which may suggest an early morning scene.

Jashar means “the upright one.” The Book of Jashar was an early collection of poetry, now lost, that is also cited in 2 Samuel 1:18 (David’s lament). The Septuagint lacks the question “Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?” here. The Septuagint of 1 Kings 8:53 cites a “book of song,” which may be the same work under a slightly different name.
Literally “as a complete day” (Hebrew keyom tamim). The time is not given in hours.
The Septuagint lacks this verse, which anticipates verse 43; verse 21 places the camp at Makkedah.
Debir means “back room” or “inner sanctuary.” It was earlier called Kiriath-sepher, “city of the book” (15:15).
Negev means “dry land,” the arid region in the south of Judah.
Kadesh-barnea means “holy place of Barnea”; it was the main oasis of the Sinai wanderings (Numbers 13:26; 32:8).

verses.text: When Jabin{a} king of Hazor{b} heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, to the king of Shimron, to the king of Achshaph,
and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth,{c} and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor{d} on the west,
to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.{e}
They came out, they and all their armies with them, a great people, as many as the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.
All these kings met by appointment, and they came and camped together at the waters of Merom{f} to fight against Israel.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Do not fear them, for tomorrow at this time I will give all of them over, slain, before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.”
So Joshua and all the people of war with him came against them suddenly by the waters of Merom and fell upon them.

Yahweh gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim,{g} and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. They struck them until they left them no survivor.
Joshua did to them as Yahweh told him. He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms.
They struck with the edge of the sword every person in it, devoting them to destruction. There was no one left who breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire.
All the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured and struck with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded.
But Israel did not burn any of the cities that stood on their mounds,{h} except Hazor alone, which Joshua burned.

All the spoil of these cities and the livestock the Israelites took as plunder for themselves. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave anyone who breathed.
Just as Yahweh had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that Yahweh had commanded Moses.
So Joshua took all that land, the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel and its lowland,
from Mount Halak,{i} which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad{j} in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death.
Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.
There was not a city that made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.

For it was from Yahweh to harden their hearts, so that they would come against Israel in battle, in order that they might be devoted to destruction and receive no mercy, but be destroyed, as Yahweh commanded Moses.

At that time Joshua came and cut off the Anakim{k} from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.
There were no Anakim left in the land of the Israelites. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.

So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that Yahweh had spoken to Moses, and Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. And the land had rest from war.

notes.text: Jabin may mean “he understands” or “he discerns.” A later Jabin king of Hazor appears in Judges 4.
Hazor probably means “enclosure” or “settlement.” It was the largest city of Canaan, north of the Sea of Galilee.
That is, the Sea of Galilee; Chinnereth may mean “harp-shaped.”
Or “the heights of Dor,” a coastal town south of Mount Carmel.
Mizpah means “watchtower” or “lookout”; so also Mizpeh in verse 8.
Merom means “height.”
Misrephoth-maim may mean “burnings at the water” (perhaps lime kilns or salt pans), or “hot springs.”
Hebrew tel; see the note at 8:28.
Halak means “smooth” or “bare.”
Baal-gad means “lord of fortune,” or “Baal of Gad” (a god of luck).
Anakim probably means “people of the neck,” that is, long-necked or tall. They were remembered as giants (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 2:10–11).

verses.text: These are the kings of the land whom the Israelites struck and whose land they took possession of beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward:

Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley, and half of Gilead, as far as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites,
and the Arabah as far as the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, eastward toward Beth-jeshimoth, and on the south below the slopes of Pisgah;{a}
and the territory of Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim,{b} who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei
and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead, to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.
Moses the servant of Yahweh and the Israelites struck them, and Moses the servant of Yahweh gave it as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites struck on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir. Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their divisions,

in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, on the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negev, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites:
the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;
the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;
the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;
the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;
the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;
the king of Hormah,{c} one; the king of Arad, one;
the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;
the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;
the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;{d}
the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;
the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;
the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;
the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;
the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim{e} in Gilgal, one;
the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.{f}

notes.text: Pisgah means “cleft” or “peak.” From its summit Moses viewed the land (Deuteronomy 34:1).
The Rephaim were an ancient people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 3:11). The word is also used for the shades of the dead.
Hormah means “devotion to destruction” (from ḥaram; Numbers 21:3).
Or “the king of Aphek in Sharon.” The Septuagint reads “the king of Ophek of Aroc.”
Goiim means “nations.” The Septuagint reads “Gei of Galilee,” which suits the northern setting (compare Isaiah 9:1).
The Septuagint lists twenty-nine kings, with differences in several names.

verses.text: Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and Yahweh said to him, “You are old and advanced in years, and very much of the land remains to be possessed.
This is the land that still remains: all the regions of the Philistines and all those of the Geshurites

(from the Shihor,{a} which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers{b} of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim
in the south; all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, as far as Aphek, to the border of the Amorites;
and the land of the Gebalites,{c} and all Lebanon toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath.{d}

All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, all the Sidonians, I myself will drive them out from before the Israelites. Only allot it to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.
Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.”
With the other half of Manasseh{e} the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them beyond the Jordan eastward, just as Moses the servant of Yahweh gave them:
from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland{f} of Medeba as far as Dibon,
and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the border of the Ammonites,
and Gilead, and the territory of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan as far as Salecah,
all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim). These Moses had struck and driven out.
But the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, and Geshur and Maacath live in the midst of Israel to this day.
Only to the tribe of Levi he gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to Yahweh, the God of Israel, are their inheritance, as he said to him.{g}
Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the Reubenites according to their clans.
Their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;
Heshbon and all its cities that are in the tableland: Dibon, Bamoth-baal,{h} Beth-baal-meon,
Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath,
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,
Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,

all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses struck with the leaders of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.
Balaam also, the son of Beor, the diviner, the Israelites killed with the sword among the rest of their slain.
The border of the Reubenites was the Jordan and its region.{i} This was the inheritance of the Reubenites according to their clans, the cities with their villages.
Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of Gad, to the Gadites, according to their clans.
Their territory was Jazer and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, as far as Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,
and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim{j} to the territory of Debir,{k}

and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth,{l} and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, with the Jordan as its boundary, as far as the end of the Sea of Chinnereth, beyond the Jordan eastward.
This is the inheritance of the Gadites according to their clans, the cities with their villages.
Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was for the half-tribe of the Manassites according to their clans.
Their territory was from Mahanaim, all Bashan, all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all Havvoth-jair,{m} which are in Bashan, sixty cities,

and half of Gilead, and Ashtaroth and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh, for half of the people of Machir according to their clans.
These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.
But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance. Yahweh, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, as he said to them.{n}

notes.text: Shihor means “black” or “the pool of Horus,” probably an eastern branch of the Nile or a stream on Egypt’s border.
Hebrew seren, a Philistine word for the rulers of their five cities; it may be related to Greek tyrannos.
That is, the people of Gebal (Byblos), on the coast north of Beirut.
Or “to the entrance of Hamath.”
Hebrew “With it,” referring back to the half-tribe of Manasseh in verse 7.
Hebrew mishor, “level land,” the plateau east of the Dead Sea; so throughout this chapter.
The Septuagint adds, “This is the division that Moses made for the Israelites in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan, by Jericho” (compare verse 32).
Bamoth-baal means “high places of Baal.”
Or “The border of the Reubenites was the Jordan, as a boundary.”
Mahanaim means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2).
Hebrew Lidbir, perhaps the same as Lo-debar (2 Samuel 9:4).
Succoth means “booths” (Genesis 33:17).
Havvoth-jair means “tent villages of Jair” (Numbers 32:41).
The Septuagint lacks this verse.

verses.text: These are the inheritances that the Israelites received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar{a} the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the Israelites distributed to them.
Their inheritance was by lot, as Yahweh had commanded through Moses, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe.
For Moses had given the inheritance of the two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.

For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, except cities to live in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their possessions.
The Israelites did as Yahweh commanded Moses, and they divided the land.

Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb{b} the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite{c} said to him, “You know what Yahweh said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.
I was forty years old when Moses the servant of Yahweh sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him back word as it was in my heart.
But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt, while I wholly followed Yahweh my God.
And Moses swore on that day, saying, ‘Surely the land on which your foot has trodden will be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed Yahweh my God.’

And now, see, Yahweh has kept me alive, as he said, these forty-five years since the time that Yahweh spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, see, I am today eighty-five years old.
I am still as strong today as I was on the day that Moses sent me. My strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going out and coming in.

Now therefore give me this hill country of which Yahweh spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that Yahweh will be with me, and I will drive them out, as Yahweh said.”
Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.
Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba.{d} Arba{e} was the greatest man among the Anakim. And the land had rest from war.

notes.text: Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Caleb means “dog,” perhaps in the sense of a loyal servant. Some connect the name with kol-lev, “whole heart,” in light of verses 8–9 and 14.
The Kenizzites were a clan related to Edom (Genesis 15:19; 36:11). Caleb’s family had been joined to the tribe of Judah.
Kiriath-arba means “city of four” or “city of Arba.”
The Septuagint reads, “The name of Hebron formerly was the city of Argob; it is the mother city of the Anakim.”
